subject: Business Models
title: Loss Leaders
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Loss Leaders.

hook.text: Costco sells rotisserie chickens at a loss. $4.99 per bird, below their cost. On purpose.

buildup.text: The chicken sits at the back of the store. To reach it, you walk past hundreds of other products.

discovery.text: Average Costco shoppers spend $136 per visit. The $4.99 chicken is bait, not the real product.

twist.text: Amazon does this with Kindle readers: sell hardware cheap, profit from book sales forever.

climax.text: Loss leaders work only when the follow-on purchase is nearly guaranteed. Without it, you just lose.

punchline.text: Lose on the chicken, win on the cart. Strategic losses work.

quiz.question: Why does Costco sell rotisserie chicken below cost?
options: To drive traffic and larger purchases

details.summary: Loss leaders are products sold below cost to attract customers who will then purchase profitable items. Grocery stores sell milk and bread at a loss to drive store visits. Game consoles launch below manufacturing cost, earning profits on game sales and subscriptions over the console's lifetime.
details.whyItMatters: Loss leader strategy demonstrates how short-term losses can create long-term profits by changing customer purchasing behavior. Retailers, hardware manufacturers, and platforms all use this technique to acquire customers cheaply.
takeaways: Products sold below cost attract customers who buy profitable items
The loss is an intentional customer acquisition investment
Success requires that loss-leader buyers also purchase high-margin products

faq.question: How do game console manufacturers profit from loss leader pricing?
faq.answer: Sony and Microsoft sell consoles below manufacturing cost to maximize installed base. They recover losses through game licensing royalties of $10-15 per game sold, online subscription services like PlayStation Plus, and accessory sales over the console's 5-7 year lifecycle.

faq.question: What risks do loss leader strategies carry?
faq.answer: Customers may buy only the loss leader without purchasing profitable items. Competitors can match the low price, creating a race to the bottom. Regulatory restrictions in some jurisdictions limit selling below cost. Cash flow pressure intensifies if profitable attach rates fall short.
